title: Per-token energy and cost benchmarking for runtime configurations
author: Ravi Menon
content:
Summary:

This document defines Redwood's methodology for measuring per-token energy consumption and mapping that to unit cost across common runtime configurations. The goal is to provide reproducible benchmarks that combine power telemetry, token accounting, latency buckets, and scheduler/kernel settings. Use these measurements to: (1) guide model/quantization selection for cost-sensitive workloads, (2) set realistic energy-aware SLOs for Dedicated pools, and (3) feed cost-model inputs for the Console optimizer recommendations.

Scope and motivation:

- Scope: LLM inference CPU/GPU stacks used by Redwood Hosted and Dedicated runtimes. Includes: model variants (fp16/int8/q4f16), sequence lengths 8–2048, batching policies, KV cache hit/miss scenarios, and multi-tenant kernel scheduling modes.
- Motivation: token-level unit cost is traditionally driven by time-on-kernel. We complement that with measured power to capture the true marginal energy cost for chargeback and optimization. This matters for large-scale Dedicated fleets and green/Sustainability metrics.

Owner and contacts:

- Owner: eng-serving-runtime / Performance Team
- Primary contact: ravi.menon@redwood.ai
- Secondary: perf-oncall@redwood.ai

Definitions and conventions:

1) Measurement interval: telemetry window aligned to a request or batch lifecycle. Default: request submission time -> last token emitted + 5ms drain.
2) Per-token energy (ET): measured joules consumed attributable to generating a token. Calculation method described below.
3) Baseline idle power (P_idle): power draw of the node(s) measured with runtime process up but quiescent (no requests, background housekeeping allowed).
4) Attribution unit: single request, or combinable into micro-batches for throughput experiments.

Hardware and software profiles used in this doc:

- GPU types: A100 80GB (nvml), A10G 24GB (nvml), H100 (nvml).
- Node configs: 1xGPU, 4xGPU NCCL-sharded nodes.
- Runtime: redwood-runtime v2.3.1 (includes kernel scheduler v1.8).
- Kernel builds: cuda-12.2 + custom attention kernel v6.1.

Measurement methodology (step-by-step):

1) Prepare test fleet:
   a) Reserve 3 identical nodes for each hardware profile.
   b) Deploy runtime build under test with identical runtime flags except for the variable under measurement (e.g., quantization flag).

2) Calibrate idle power (P_idle):
   a) Remove user traffic and ensure collector is attached (nvml-exporter or node-power-proxy).
   b) Collect power for 120s and store median as P_idle_node.

3) Generate traffic workload:
   a) Use workload runner (perf-runner v1.5) with a representative prompt set. Include: small-chat (len 16), search-snippet (len 128), long-form (len 1024).
   b) For each request profile, run 10,000 requests for stable averages. Use fixed seed for deterministic tokenization.

4) Collect telemetry:
   a) Power telemetry: sample at 100Hz from NVML via node export.
   b) Runtime telemetry: token counts, kernel invocation timestamps, kernel IDs, batch sizes, and KV-cache hit ratio.
   c) Infrastructure telemetry: CPU utilization, PCIe bandwidth counters, GPU memory usage.

5) Compute per-token energy (ET):
   a) For each request window, compute energy_joules = SUM_over_samples(power_sample - P_idle_node) * sample_interval_seconds.
   b) ET_request = energy_joules / tokens_emitted_in_request.
   c) Aggregate across requests to produce mean, median, and 99th-percentile ET per workload bucket.

6) Convert energy to cost:
   a) Input parameters: cost_per_kWh (team finance input), datacenter PUE, currency.
   b) cost_per_joule = cost_per_kWh / (3600 * 1000).
   c) token_cost = ET_request * cost_per_joule * PUE.

Minimum reproducibility checklist (run before publishing results):

- [ ] Node clock sync verified (chrony/ntp).
- [ ] nvml-exporter version logged and consistent across nodes.
- [ ] Workload runner commit hash recorded.
- [ ] Kernel build id and runtime version recorded.
- [ ] P_idle measurement attached.
- [ ] At least 3 nodes per profile used with cross-node variance reported.

Observations from initial runs (summary):

- Quantization (q4/q8) reduces per-token energy by 20%–45% depending on GPU and sequence length; savings are largest on memory-bound long sequences where reduced memory traffic reduces PCIe and cache thrash.
- Batch coalescing increases tokens/s but can increase peak power draw; net per-token energy often decreases for medium-length sequences because kernel amortization dominates.
- KV-cache hits reduce ET per token by ~10% for long-form generation due to fewer recomputed attention kernels.
- Scheduler mode matters: ‘‘preemptive-strict’’ reduces tail ET variance by enforcing kernel preemption at a small latency cost; ‘‘greedy-batch’’ yields lower mean ET but higher P99.

Recommended reporting format for dashboards and Console integration:

- Fields to expose per model-config: mean_ET_j, p50_ET_j, p95_ET_j, p99_ET_j, tokens_per_second, mean_latency_ms, token_cost_usd_1e-6, hardware_profile, kernel_build, runtime_version, sample_size.
- Expose an annotation for any measurement where KV-cache behavior is >90% hit or variance on P_idle >5%.

Common pitfalls and mitigations:

- Pitfall: Idle measurement drift due to background system jobs. Mitigation: pin collector to cgroup and exclude telemetry windows where system CPU >5%.
- Pitfall: NVML sampling aliasing with kernel bursts -> undercounting of short spikes. Mitigation: increase NVML sampling to 200Hz for short-burst tests or use direct power-sampling kernel.
- Pitfall: Tokenization differences across tokenizer versions causing token count mismatches. Mitigation: freeze tokenizer commit used for each benchmark and include tokenizer hash in results.

Actionable tuning checklist (for operators):

1) If per-token energy is higher than baseline by >30% for a given model-config:
   - Validate that kernel build matches the recommended kernel list (see "approved-kernels.txt").
   - Check for memory thrashing on GPU (mem_util > 95% for sustained periods).
   - If model is memory-bound, try quantized variant or increase batch size if latency budget allows.

2) If P99 ET is high (>2x mean):
   - Investigate scheduler preemption mode and noisy neighbors.
   - Run single-tenant microbench to isolate kernel scheduling effects.

3) If tokens/s is unexpectedly low after a runtime upgrade:
   - Compare kernel timings across two builds using kernel-trace profile.
   - Rollback to previous kernel candidate if regression persists, and open a kernel-bisect ticket.

How this feeds into product decisions and Console optimizations:

- Pricing: token_cost estimates feed into Dedicated capacity pricing simulations. Use mean token_cost for baseline price and p95 for SLO reserve.
- Autoscaling heuristics: energy-aware policies can prefer lower-energy nodes during non-peak windows to reduce cost without violating throughput SLOs.
- Model recommendations: Optimize will prefer a model/quantization combo that minimizes token_cost while meeting latency SLO.

Example CLI snippets and reproducibility artifacts:

- Start power collector:
  ./tools/node-power-proxy --nvml --sample-rate 100 --out /tmp/power-node-1.csv

- Run workload runner (example):
  perf-runner run --workload small-chat-16 --concurrency 64 --requests 10000 --seed 42 --out /tmp/results-small-chat-16.json

- Compute ET (example one-liner):
  python tools/et_calc.py --power /tmp/power-node-1.csv --telemetry /tmp/results-small-chat-16.json --p_idle 75 --out /tmp/et-small-chat.csv

Appendix A: Example cost conversion parameters (finance input)

- cost_per_kWh = $0.06
- PUE = 1.2
- cost_per_joule = 0.06 / 3,600,000 = 1.67e-8 USD/J
